children: Concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence on brokerage firms have repeatedly driven selloffs in those firms' stocks. On Tuesday, the sector took a licking, this time because of worries about Facebook parent Meta's new personal AI assistant, Muse.

Shares of Charles Schwab dropped 6% on Tuesday, its largest percentage decrease since April 16. LPL Financial and Raymond James Financial fell 7.4% and 3.5%, respectively, amid a broader selloff in financial stocks.

Those three stocks saw more muted activity on Wednesday, with Schwab down 0.2% early in the afternoon, LPL up 0.1%, and Raymond James down 0.3%. The Vanguard Financials ETF was down 0.1%. The benchmark S&P 500 index was down 0.8%.

Meta says Muse, which has surged to the top spot in Apple's app store, can help users with a range of tasks, including sending emails, booking travel, and making purchases. Meta unveiled Muse earlier this month.

Investors' concern about Muse centers on whether it or other AI tools may eventually help investors automatically move idle cash out of low-paying sweep accounts at brokerage firms to higher-paying options, such as high-yield savings accounts and money-market funds. That could put a dent in profits at Schwab, LPL, and other companies that generate handsome net interest income from sweep accounts. NII is the difference between what financial services companies pay in interest on customer deposits and what they earn on interest-bearing assets, such as loans.

The potential stakes for brokerage firms are higher in this elevated interest-rate environment, Truist analyst David Smith writes in a Sept. 22 research note. That means customers have stronger incentives to move idle dollars from low-paying sweep accounts to higher-yielding accounts.

There are hurdles, however, to a hypothetical "max cash sorting" scenario becoming reality, Smith says. Cash balances in sweep accounts are unlikely to go to zero because customers will want to keep dry powder handy for investing opportunities. In addition, some Schwab rivals have offered high-yield savings and brokerage accounts for years, and that hasn't meaningfully hindered Schwab's asset growth, he adds. Plus, brokerage firms aren't without options. If their profits on sweep cash drop, they can make up for it by charging more for other services.

Smith gives Schwab's stock a Buy rating; he rates LPL and Raymond James Financial stocks Hold. His research note points out that Robinhood Markets is at relatively little risk from AI-cash concerns because the brokerage firm already pays a near-market yield on customer cash.

The Muse-related selloff isn't the first time AI concerns have weighed on brokerage and wealth management stocks. In May, those stocks sold off after JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said his company was working on an AI-cash optimization tool. In February, shares of Schwab and other companies plunged following the launch of new AI-powered tax-planning tools by fintech company Altruist. (In August, asset manager Vanguard agreed to buy Altruist.) The stocks recovered in the weeks that followed in part because tailwinds are benefiting the sector. Trading activity has remained robust and customers continue to open new brokerage accounts and add funds to existing accounts. For example, Schwab raked in $120 billion in core net new assets in the second quarter. That was up from $74 billion for the same period a year ago.

Brokerage firms have also continued to emphasize the ways in which they are using artificial intelligence to improve efficiency and boost business. Last week, Schwab announced that it was joining with Anthropic to provide the technology company's expanding suite of tools to the thousands of registered investment advisors that Schwab serves.

In a Sept. 22 research note, TD Cowen analyst Bill Katz says that AI-related cash-sorting concerns will take time to dispel. He is also "watchful" for the potential AI commoditization of advice at the lower end of the mass market.
Because AI is a new technology, investors need time to ruminate on how it may remake industries. Brokerage stocks' AI odyssey is far from over.
